title: What C Is and How It Runs
relevance: SDE interviews probe whether you understand C as a close-to-hardware systems language, the compile/link pipeline, and what undefined behavior actually means.

phases.goal: Establish what C is for, how standards matter, and the shape of a hosted first program.

must_hit.point: C is a small, fast, close-to-the-hardware systems language that provides minimal abstraction and trusts the programmer completely.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions systems use cases (kernels, firmware, drivers) and that C sits close to the machine with little abstraction.

must_hit.point: C evolved from informal K&R C through ANSI C (C89/C90), then C99, C11, C17, and recently C23; the chosen -std flag dictates available language features and library functions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the standards sequence and says -std=c17 or similar controls which features you get.

must_hit.point: In a hosted C program, int main(void) is the entry point; return 0; passes process exit status to the OS, and by convention 0 means success.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains main as entry, return value as exit status, and 0 as success.

must_hit.point: By default every C program has three standard streams: stdin, stdout, and stderr.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the three streams and their roles (input, normal output, errors).

probes: What is C designed for, and why do people still use it instead of higher-level languages?
What standard of C do you typically target, and why does it matter?

hints.1: Think about where performance, determinism, and direct memory access matter.
hints.2: Separate philosophy (minimal abstraction) from standards (what -std unlocks) and from the hello-world entry/exit contract.
hints.3: C is close-to-hardware systems C from Bell Labs Unix era; standards run K&R → C89/C90 → C99 → C11 → C17 → C23; main returns an int exit status where 0 means success.

phases.goal: Explain how source becomes an executable and how the abstract machine categorizes behavior.

must_hit.point: gcc as a driver orchestrates four stages: preprocessing (comments stripped, macros expanded, #include pasted), compilation to assembly, assembly to an object file, then linking into an executable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the four stages in order and distinguishes object files from the final linked binary.

must_hit.point: A translation unit is one .c file after the preprocessor expands macros and pastes includes; an object file holds machine code for one translation unit but may still have unresolved external references.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines translation unit vs object file and notes linking resolves externals like printf.

must_hit.point: The C standard describes an Abstract Machine; observable program behavior is categorized as well-defined, implementation-defined, unspecified, or undefined.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the abstract machine and all four behavior buckets with a short example for each.

must_hit.point: An ABI is the low-level contract between a binary and the OS/hardware (e.g., data layout and which registers pass arguments); a native binary is bound to a CPU architecture and OS, so other targets need cross-compilation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines ABI and connects it to why binaries are not portable across architecture/OS without a matching toolchain.

probes: Walk me through what happens when you run gcc main.c -o myprogram.
What is undefined behavior, and how is it different from implementation-defined behavior?

hints.1: Treat the build like an assembly line with intermediate products between stages.
hints.2: Cover preprocess → compile → assemble → link, then the four behavior categories under the abstract machine.
hints.3: Preprocess pastes/expands text; compile emits assembly; assemble makes .o; link resolves externals. UB means the standard imposes no requirements; implementation-defined means the compiler must choose and document one option.

phases.goal: Surface the costs of native compilation and why the standard leaves some choices open.

must_hit.point: C compiles to native machine code with no software intermediary, buying maximum performance and minimal overhead but costing portability versus interpreted languages.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts native execution/performance with being tied to architecture and OS.

must_hit.point: Implementation-defined behavior lets compilers choose among allowed options and document them (e.g., size of int), rather than forcing every compiler to do exactly the same thing.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says the standard deliberately leaves some choices to the implementation for platform fit, with documentation required.

must_hit.point: Compilation and linking are separate so each translation unit can become an object file whose external references are resolved later when multiple objects and libraries are stitched together.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains separate compilation: compile units independently, then link to resolve symbols across files and libraries.

probes: Why split compilation and linking instead of compiling straight to an executable?
Why does the C standard allow implementation-defined behavior instead of mandating identical behavior everywhere?

hints.1: Compare what you gain from native code with what you give up.
hints.2: Tie performance/portability to ABI binding, and tie implementation-defined choices to hardware differences.
hints.3: Native code is fast but architecture/OS-specific; separate link step resolves externals across .o files; implementation-defined (documented choice) exists so compilers can match real machines.

phases.goal: Show practical compiler flags, stage-stop switches, and how pipeline failures surface.

must_hit.point: A robust baseline build uses flags like -std=c17, -Wall -Wextra, -O2, and -g; -E/-S/-c stop after preprocess, assembly text, or object-file stages respectively.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names several of those flags and what artifact each stop flag produces.

must_hit.point: Syntax errors fail compilation; a declared but undefined function can compile yet fail at link time with an undefined reference.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes compile-time syntax failure from linker undefined-reference when a definition is missing.

must_hit.point: Inspecting the pipeline: gcc -E expands headers/macros into huge text; gcc -S yields .s assembly; gcc -c yields a binary .o; linking the .o with the C library produces the executable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes what you see in .i/.s/.o and that linking connects calls like puts to the system C library.

probes: How would you inspect what the preprocessor or assembler produced for a simple hello.c?
If the compiler succeeds but the linker reports undefined reference, what went wrong?

hints.1: Think about flags that stop the driver early versus a full link.
hints.2: Map -E, -S, -c, and full link to text, assembly, object, and executable artifacts.
hints.3: Use -E for expanded source, -S for .s, -c for .o; missing function definitions break the linker with undefined reference even when compilation of the caller succeeded.

tradeoffs.topic: Native compiled C vs interpreted languages
tradeoffs.strong_answer: C produces raw machine instructions the CPU runs directly—maximum performance and minimal overhead—but the binary is bound to a target CPU architecture and OS, unlike more portable interpreted runtimes.

tradeoffs.topic: Separate compilation and linking vs compile-straight-to-executable
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Compiling to object files per translation unit, then linking, lets the toolchain resolve external references across multiple .o files and libraries (e.g., printf/puts in the C library) instead of requiring one monolithic compile-to-executable step.

tradeoffs.topic: Implementation-defined behavior vs mandating identical compiler behavior
tradeoffs.strong_answer: The standard allows a documented choice among options (such as the size of int) so implementations can fit real hardware, rather than forcing every compiler to behave identically in every low-level detail.

gotchas.trap: Treating #include like a Python-style module import.
gotchas.correction: #include is literal text inclusion; a large header is fully processed by the compiler every time that translation unit is compiled.

gotchas.trap: Assuming undefined behavior means the program will crash or return garbage.
gotchas.correction: UB means the standard imposes no requirements; the compiler may assume the invalid code never happens and can delete checks, break earlier code, or do anything else.

gotchas.trap: Expecting a missing function definition to fail at compile time.
gotchas.correction: Declaring a function without defining it can compile; the linker fails later with an undefined reference if no object provides the definition.
